summary: Describes Virtual Private LAN Service, a Layer 2 VPN that joins customer sites into one multipoint Ethernet LAN over a provider network. It uses BGP to discover which sites belong together and to set up the connections.

plainLanguage.summary: VPLS connects Ethernet sites across a provider network so they can act like one multipoint LAN. This RFC uses BGP to find the participating provider routers and establish their pseudowires.

questions: how does bgp vpls auto-discovery work
what is a vpls label block
subtitle: How BGP discovers VPLS members and signals the labels used to connect their Ethernet sites.

tldr.problem: A provider needs to connect customer Ethernet sites as one multipoint LAN without configuring every provider edge router with every other member.
tldr.mechanism: BGP announcements identify VPLS membership and carry label blocks used to establish pseudowires. Provider edge routers learn MAC addresses and forward frames like a learning bridge.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines BGP-based discovery and signaling. It is distinct from and incompatible with the LDP-based VPLS method in RFC 4762, and RFC 4761 has been updated by RFC 5462, RFC 8395, and RFC 8614.

today: RFC 4761 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 5462, RFC 8395, and RFC 8614. Its BGP-signaled method is distinct from and incompatible with the LDP-signaled method in RFC 4762.

sections.title: A Multipoint Ethernet Service
sections.content:
Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) joins customer sites across a packet-switched provider network so the sites appear as one Ethernet LAN. The provider network uses pseudowires to connect its edge devices and performs MAC learning, flooding, and forwarding for each VPLS.

This RFC defines the service model, BGP-based member discovery and signaling, frame forwarding, and deployment options. The RFC's IESG note distinguishes this BGP method from the LDP-based VPLS method in RFC 4762; the two methods are incompatible.
sections.plainLanguage: VPLS connects distant customer Ethernet sites as one multipoint LAN. Provider routers use pseudowires to carry frames between those sites.

sections.title: Provider and Customer Roles
sections.content:
Customer Edge (CE) devices connect to Provider Edge (PE) routers or to VPLS-aware layer-two aggregation devices called u-PEs. A CE does not need to know that VPLS is in use; it behaves as though it is connected to the other CEs through a switched LAN.

The RFC assumes participating PEs have a logical full mesh of bidirectional pseudowires for each VPLS. The tunnels carrying those pseudowires may use IP or MPLS, and their setup is outside this document.

A PE can participate in VPLS and IP VPN services at the same time, but it keeps their routing information separate. They can share underlying tunnels.
sections.plainLanguage: Customer devices connect to provider edge devices and need no special awareness of the virtual LAN. The provider's PEs connect to one another through pseudowires.

sections.title: Finding Members with BGP
sections.content:
Without auto-discovery, every PE would need the identities of the other PEs in its VPLS. With auto-discovery, a PE is configured with its own VPLS membership and learns about other members through BGP.

A Route Target extended community identifies a VPLS. A PE announces membership with that Route Target and accepts matching announcements. It withdraws its announcements when it leaves the VPLS.

The BGP update carries both membership information and signaling details. When a PE receives a matching announcement, it learns that the remote PE is a member and sets up its part of the pseudowire. BGP does not exchange MAC addresses; each PE learns them in its data plane.
sections.plainLanguage: Each PE announces the VPLS identifier it belongs to. Other PEs with the same identifier discover one another and set up pseudowires.

sections.title: Label Blocks and the VPLS Announcement
sections.content:
A label block lets one announcement provide labels for multiple remote VEs. It contains a label base, a VE block offset, and a VE block size. A receiving VE uses its own VE ID to select the label for traffic sent to the announcing PE.

The VPLS BGP Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI) carries a Route Distinguisher, VE ID, block offset, block size, and label base. The RFC assigns it the L2VPN address family and VPLS subsequent address family values.

A Layer2 Info Extended Community carries the encapsulation type, control flags, and layer-two MTU. Its flags indicate whether a control word and sequenced delivery are required.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of announcing one label per remote router, a PE announces a block. Each remote VE uses its identifier to calculate the label that reaches that PE.

sections.title: Learning and Forwarding Ethernet Frames
sections.content:
Each PE acts as part of a logical learning bridge for its VPLS. It records which logical port a source MAC address arrived on, then uses that information to forward later frames for that address.

When a destination address is unknown, a PE floods the frame to the other VEs in the VPLS. Broadcast frames are also sent to all stations. Split-horizon forwarding prevents a PE from sending a frame received from another PE onward to other PEs, because the originating PE already sent it to them.

Learning can use only the MAC address or the customer VLAN tag together with the MAC address. These choices trade a single broadcast domain against more selective forwarding and larger MAC tables.
sections.plainLanguage: Provider edge devices learn which port reaches each source address. They flood unknown destinations, but do not send a received frame back toward other PEs that already received it.

sections.title: Multiple Provider Networks and Redundant Sites
sections.content:
When a VPLS crosses autonomous-system boundaries, the RFC describes three signaling approaches. One makes border routers act as PEs and requires Ethernet and VPLS state there. Another exchanges VPLS information between border routers and uses MPLS. A third uses multihop external BGP between PEs or route reflectors and keeps VPLS state off the border routers.

A site may connect to more than one PE. If those PEs use the same VE ID, BGP path selection chooses one equivalent announcement. If they use different VE IDs, the RFC requires spanning tree at the CE to build a loop-free topology.

Route reflectors reduce the need for a full mesh of BGP sessions. They affect the control plane and do not add VPLS data-plane forwarding state.
sections.plainLanguage: VPLS can cross provider-network boundaries using several BGP arrangements. Redundant site connections need a loop-free choice, made by BGP path selection or by spanning tree depending on the VE IDs.

sections.title: Privacy Is Not Encryption
sections.content:
VPLS aims to keep a customer's frames within that VPLS, but it does not provide confidentiality, integrity, or authentication. Packets cross the provider network in the clear, where a party with access to the path may eavesdrop or inject traffic.

The RFC suggests IPsec for PE-to-PE tunnels or encryption by the customer systems before data enters the provider network. Authenticating BGP sessions can make spoofed updates and withdrawals harder, but it does not hide VPLS labels.

A wrong Route Target can connect customer sites from different VPLSs. For MPLS-in-IP or MPLS-in-GRE tunnels, implementations must provide IPsec or allow the egress PE to validate the source address.
sections.plainLanguage: VPLS separates traffic by service but does not encrypt it. Use encryption when confidentiality is needed, and protect BGP and tunnel traffic against false updates and packets.
